name: Swamp / bayou
notes: Warm-temperate to subtropical forested wetland: flood-tolerant cypress-tupelo canopy on permanently or seasonally inundated soil, willow and buttonbush fringe, duckweed and floating plants, Spanish moss. Drawn on the Louisiana bayous, Okefenokee, Florida cypress domes and the Pantanal/Amazon varzea fringe.

canopy.name: Bald cypress

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: 3-9 (usually 6) cotyledons, then soft, flat, feathery needles in two ranks on deciduous side shoots; seedlings grow 20-75 cm in their first year if not flooded over. The sapling is a slender, pyramidal cone; buttress and knees come later and the crown flattens with age. Foliage turns copper-red and drops in autumn.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of N. America (seedlings 20-75 cm in year 1; soil saturated but not flooded 1-3 months for germination; intermediate shade tolerance; height growth stops ~200 yr); Wikipedia (3 m at 5 yr, 21 m at 41 yr, 36 m at 96 yr; seed from ~30 yr; 3-9 cotyledons; Black River tree at least 2,624 yr old).

canopy.source: SE US swamps and river bottoms; deciduous conifer; knees; 1,000+ years. Kew POWO.

canopy.name: Moriche palm

growth.juvenile_note: The seed sends a germination tube down into the wet soil from which the seedling rises. The first leaves are simple, strap-like pleated blades; later leaves turn into huge rounded costapalmate fans on long stalks. For years it is a stemless tuft of fans in the swamp while the trunk base thickens underground, then a smooth grey column rises and old leaves fall cleanly away.

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: seeds germinate on mud once floodwater falls; two oblong cotyledons, then large, oval, glossy leaves, sometimes with a few coarse teeth. The seedling is a straight single stem that survives flooding all season; saplings are slender whips with a narrow crown, and in the swamp the base later swells into a big buttressed, bottle-shaped trunk.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of N. America vol. 2 (Nyssa aquatica: seed from ~30 yr or 20 cm dbh, sprouts at 2 yr; good crops yearly; 30-yr trees ~23 m on good sites, SI 21-27 m at 50 yr; intolerant of shade; seeds germinate when water recedes; long-lived); Woody Plant Seed Manual (epigeal; 87% germination in 21 days)

canopy.name: Red maple

growth.juvenile_note: Seed falls in late spring and most of it germinates at once on wet mud or moss (some waits a year). Epigeal: two strap-shaped cotyledons, then opposite, coarsely toothed, shallowly three-lobed leaves on red stalks. A slender whip with red twigs that survives years under a canopy and races up in a gap; cut or burned stems resprout as a clump of several stems, the usual multi-trunked swamp form.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 2 (Walters & Yawney, Acer rubrum): seed ripens and is dispersed April-July and germinates soon after; seed from about age 4; rarely lives beyond 150 yr; tolerant of shade; vigorous stump sprouting

repro.note: flowers by insects and wind before the leaves; samaras spin on the wind; stumps and burned stems resprout

canopy.name: Fever tree

growth.juvenile_note: Hot-water-soaked seed sprouts quickly; seedlings have two oval cotyledons, reach the two-leaf stage in 6-8 weeks and carry feathery bipinnate leaves and pairs of straight white spines. Young trees shoot up 1-1.5 m a year as slender single-stemmed whips, and the powdery greenish-yellow bark that names the tree shows early; the flat-topped crown spreads later.
growth.source: SANBI PlantZAfrica (Vachellia xanthophloea): 15-25 m, about 1.5 m a year under ideal conditions, seed soaked overnight in hot water, two-leaf stage 6-8 weeks after sowing, dappled shade below; ICRAF Agroforestree: 1-1.5 m a year. First flowering, lifespan and height curve estimated.

canopy.source: African river margins and pans; yellow bark. Kew POWO (African acacias are now Vachellia/Senegalia; Acacia is the Australian wattles). Thorny (African), flat crowns, insect-pollinated, pods eaten by browsers which spread the seed; giraffe and goat browse; fire-adapted.

growth.source: USDA FEIS (Typha latifolia): germinates best at 25-30 C in high light; 2-4 small then 2-6 floating leaves before erect ones; seedlings 60-85 cm after 84 d; flowers early in 2nd year; ramets die within a year, rhizomes live about 2 yr; one seedling's rhizomes spread 3 m in a season; shade intolerant.

ground.name: Royal fern

growth.juvenile_note: Short-lived green spores germinate within 1-3 days into heart-shaped prothalli on wet mud; the first fronds are tiny, fan-shaped and lobed, then once-pinnate. Over several years it builds a tufted crown of tall, bipinnate, pale-green fronds with oblong leaflets; new fronds unroll coppery-red and woolly, and fertile tips carry rust-brown, flower-like spore clusters.
growth.source: SANBI PlantZAfrica (green spores germinate within a day; grows in shade or full sun if wet; 1.5 m, to 3.3 m in Europe); Illinois Wildflowers (spreads slowly, crowns live to ~100 years); years to full size and first fertile fronds estimated from Osmundaceae cultivation

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.name: Taro

growth.juvenile_note: Almost always grows from a corm or side cormel (true seed is rare): a pointed shoot unrolls into a small rosette of long-stalked leaves. Blades are heart- to arrow-shaped and peltate (stalk joined inside the blade), velvety and water-repellent; each new leaf is bigger until the clump of 'elephant ear' leaves on 1 m stalks is reached in 5-7 months, with cormels budding around the base.

growth.juvenile_note: Seed is seldom viable; new plants come almost entirely from long creeping rhizomes, which send up single erect leafy culms at intervals so that a stand spreads as an even sward over shallow water and wet peat.
growth.source: USDA FEIS (Panicum hemitomon: spreads by rhizomes, seed production low and viability poor, resprouts after fire); Flora of North America vol. 25

repro.note: flowers sparsely; stands are clonal from rhizomes

ground.source: Panicum hemitomon, maidencane (Poaceae); accepted in Flora of North America and USDA Plants (some recent work moves it to a segregate genus; Kew POWO status not checked here). Coastal plain from New Jersey to Florida and Texas; dominant of the Okefenokee 'prairies' and of Florida and Louisiana freshwater marsh and cypress-dome margins; 0.5-1.8 m, rhizomatous — Flora of North America vol. 25; USDA FEIS.

leaf.notes: flat bright green blades 5-15 mm wide spaced up erect stems

flower.form: narrow spike-like panicle 10-30 cm, rarely produced

appearance.seasonal: green spring to autumn; tops straw-brown in winter
appearance.silhouette: even waist-high green grass sward over shallow water
appearance.refs: Flora of North America vol. 25; USDA FEIS; Wikipedia Panicum hemitomon

leaf.note: flat blades 5-15 mm wide along erect culms

ground.name: American tree moss

growth.juvenile_note: A spore grows into a green thread (protonema) that buds a creeping underground stem; from it rise upright shoots, bare below, that branch at the top into a little tree-like tuft. Colonies spread by the creeping stems over wet soil, logs and tree bases.
growth.source: Crum & Anderson, Mosses of Eastern North America (1981): Climacium americanum, dendroid from creeping stolons, on wet soil and rotten wood in swamps

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Climacium americanum, American tree moss (Climaciaceae), accepted; Quebec and Ontario to Florida and Texas, on wet soil, rotting wood and the bases of trees in swamps and bottomland forest (Mike's 'cypress-knee moss'); dendroid shoots 3-10 cm — Crum & Anderson 1981; Flora of North America vol. 28.

leaf.notes: upright wiry stems 3-10 cm, bare below, branching at the top into a crowded tuft like a miniature tree; yellowish green, glossy when wet

fruit.form: reddish-brown cylindrical capsules on long stalks, autumn to winter

appearance.silhouette: lawn of tiny green trees on wet ground and tree bases
appearance.refs: Crum & Anderson 1981; Flora of North America vol. 28

leaf.note: branch leaves ovate-lanceolate, pleated, toothed toward the tip, single costa

ground.silhouette: lawn of tiny green trees on wet ground and tree bases

ground.name: Feathery bog-moss

growth.juvenile_note: Spores and broken shoot fragments start new plants in open pools; one of the fastest-growing peat mosses, it fills a hollow within a few seasons with limp, feathery, submerged plumes that thicken into a floating yellow-green carpet.
growth.source: British Bryological Society field guide (Sphagnum cuspidatum: submerged and floating in acid pools, 'drowned kitten' aquatic form); Bengtsson et al. 2016 (hollow sphagna grow fastest)

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Sphagnum cuspidatum, feathery bog-moss (Sphagnaceae), accepted; Europe and eastern North America down the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain, submerged and floating in acid pools, hollows and swamp margins (its presence in the Okefenokee and Gulf swamps is estimated from the coastal-plain range) — BBS Field Guide; Flora of North America vol. 27.

leaf.notes: long narrow curved branch leaves; under water the shoots are limp feathery plumes, out of it a yellow-green carpet that bleaches pale as the pool drops

appearance.seasonal: evergreen; bleaches pale when the water falls
appearance.silhouette: yellow-green feathery mats filling dark swamp pools
appearance.refs: BBS Field Guide; Flora of North America vol. 27

ground.name: Brown wood ear fungus

repro.note: The mycelium is the organism and lives in the substrate for years; the mushroom is a days-long fruiting body. 'rhizome' here = the mycelium spreading through connected dead wood or litter; 'wind' = spores.

ground.source: Auricularia fuscosuccinea, a wood ear (Auriculariaceae), Index Fungorum accepted; subtropical and tropical Americas, in the US along the Gulf coast from Florida to Louisiana and Texas, on dead hardwood in swamps and bottomlands (Mike's 'cypress knee fungus') — Looney, Birkebak & Matheny 2013, Mycologia 105; Index Fungorum.

cap.form: ear- to cup-shaped rubbery gelatinous lobes attached at one side
cap.notes: translucent cinnamon- to amber-brown ears in clusters; shrivel hard and dark when dry and revive after rain

underside.type: smooth to faintly veined spore surface, no gills

appearance.habit: clusters on dead branches and logs
appearance.seasonal: fruits after warm rains; dries and revives
appearance.silhouette: brown rubbery ears lining a fallen branch

ground.name: Swamp polypore

repro.note: The mycelium is the organism and lives in the substrate for years; the mushroom is a days-long fruiting body. 'rhizome' here = the mycelium spreading through connected dead wood or litter; 'wind' = spores.

ground.source: Inonotus ludovicianus (Hymenochaetaceae), Index Fungorum; named from Louisiana, on the Gulf coastal plain and in the Southeast, an annual bracket at the bases of living and dead oaks in bottomland and swamp forest — Gilbertson & Ryvarden, North American Polypores (1986); MushroomExpert.com.

cap.notes: annual; yellow-brown with a bright yellowish margin when fresh, darkening to rusty brown and blackish; flesh rusty brown

traits.leaf_shape: strap or rosette leaves in a clump on a branch

bark.note: clustered olive-green pseudobulbs with papery tan sheaths

epiphyte.silhouette: small tufted clump on a limb

growth.juvenile_note: Dust-like seed germinates with a fungus into a tiny protocorm in bark crevices of live oak, pond apple or cypress. The young plant is a small tuft of dark-green, egg-shaped pseudobulbs about 7 cm tall, each with one or two narrow, grass-like leaves up to 16 cm, spreading into a clump that sends up wiry sprays of small green-bronze flowers with a white, purple-spotted lip.
growth.source: Wikipedia Encyclia tampensis (epiphyte; pseudobulbs ~7 cm; leaves to 16 x 2 cm; summer flowers 2.5 cm, green to bronze with white purple-dotted lip; mainly on southern live oak, also pond apple, mangroves, bald cypress; hammocks and riversides of Florida, Bahamas, Cuba). Timings estimated from Encyclia culture.

epiphyte.name: Ghost orchid

growth.juvenile_note: Dust-like seed germinates only with a specific fungus into a tiny protocorm on the bark of pond apple or pop ash. The plant never makes real leaves: the young orchid is a few flat, grey-green photosynthetic roots radiating from a minute stem, slowly spreading into a flat root web 18-20 cm across before it can flower.
growth.source: Wikipedia Dendrophylax lindenii (leafless, leaves reduced to scales; flowers only once the root mass is ~180-200 mm across; flowers Jun-Aug, white, 3-4 x 7-9 cm; hawkmoth-pollinated; on Annona glabra and Fraxinus caroliniana in swamp forest; seedlings very hard to raise). Years to flowering and lifespan estimated.

repro.note: dust seed by wind; germinates only where its fungus lives (reads mycorrhizal presence); most species need one specific pollinator

epiphyte.source: Florida and Cuban swamp forest. Leafless roots on pond apple and cypress; sphinx-moth pollinated at night. Kew POWO.

epiphyte.name: Resurrection fern
epiphyte.source: Pleopeltis polypodioides, resurrection fern, epiphytic on live oak and cypress limbs SE USA — Wikipedia

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

bark.note: creeping rhizome clothed in brown scales; short green stipes

epiphyte.silhouette: furry green mat along horizontal limbs

growth.juvenile_note: Spores sprout on moss and bark of oak limbs into tiny heart-shaped prothalli; the first fronds are small, simple to shallowly lobed and leathery, then once-pinnatifid fronds with grey-scaly undersides. A slender creeping rhizome (about 2 mm thick) branches along the bark into a mat. In drought the fronds curl up grey-brown and look dead, turning green again within a day or two of rain.
growth.source: Wikipedia Pleopeltis polypodioides (fronds to 25 x 5 cm; rhizome 2 mm; survives losing up to 97% of its water and rehydrates in 24-48 h; spores summer to autumn; rhizome pieces root). Spore-to-plant time, growth and lifespan estimated from epiphytic Polypodiaceae.

epiphyte.note_habit: 1 Oct (Mike's play): an EPIPHYTE — a creeping mat of small leathery fronds on the upper side of big limbs, classically live oak, also cypress, other hardwoods and rock; never ground cover. 'Resurrection': in a dry spell the fronds curl and go grey-brown and can lose most of their water, then green and unfurl within hours of rain. The tropical dry forest copy had it in the ground tier, and as the first file loaded it set the tier for the whole game; all four copies now agree.

desiccation.source: Pleopeltis polypodioides: poikilohydric, desiccation-tolerant; in drought the fronds roll inward and show the grey-brown, densely scaled underside, and can lose up to ~97 % of their water; rehydrated by rain they flatten and turn green within hours, fully within about a day (USDA Forest Service / university extension accounts; Stuart 1968; Muslin & Homann 1992)
desiccation._note: Design 1 Oct §CD (Mike: it behaves as it does in real life). wet_rain_mm_h: local rain (WeatherSim.local_weather) at or above this counts as wetting. Dry: after curl_starts_game_h without rain the fronds begin to roll; by dry_after_game_days they are fully rolled (dry_curl 0-1) and dry_color with the scaly underside showing (dry_underside_shows). Rain: unfurling starts within unfurl_starts_game_h and the plant is flat and green by green_after_game_h. humidity_slows: fog and high humidity stretch the drying. dormant_when_dry: no growth while dry. First guesses on real timings; the designer tunes.
